text: After his dinner with Lake, Daugherty began working the phones. He talked with Cyrus Western, the head of EPA’s Rocky Mountain region; state legislators in Cheyenne; Republican Sen. Cynthia Lummis; and even “diesel influencers” on social media (“Troy had an army of mullets behind him,” Daugherty joked.) Lake and his wife had a relationship with two veterans who knew EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin from his time as an Army officer, “so they made phone calls on behalf of the Lakes, and within a half an hour we had an appointment with Sean Hayes,” the deputy White House counsel who works closely on pardons, Daugherty said. Things were quiet for a while, and then last November, without warning, Daugherty got a call from Lummis’ office confirming Lake had been pardoned. They went to a celebratory dinner at the Little Bear Inn in Cheyenne, where Lake’s son used Daugherty’s pocket knife to slice off his ankle monitor. The tracking agency called immediately, Daugherty said, and Lake explained the president had just pardoned him. “They expressed the same astonishment and congratulated him, but said, ‘We need to hear it from someone but you,’ so we put them in touch with the proper authorities, and it was really magical,” Daugherty said. (Lake unsuccessfully tried to purchase the severed monitor to keep as a trophy.) Lake’s story apparently resonated with the president.
